description: Étudiants camerounais en ingénierie, nous concevons un logiciel visuel de surveillance de la santé des astronautes : silhouette humaine interactive, code couleur, graphiques d'évolution et conseils simples, utilisable hors ligne. Nous travaillons de façon méthodique. Nous recherchons des profils motivés, idéalement en design UI/UX, développement front-end (React), santé ou physiologie, analyse de données ou communication. Rejoignez-nous pour créer un outil utile et sérieux !
summary:
We designed smart health glasses for astronauts on long missions, focused on immune health. The glasses are a concept: their sensors (temperature, resting pulse, cabin CO2) are simulated on a computer, while sleep, symptoms and blood test values are logged by voice.

We built a hands-free assistant on a retrieval system fed with NASA Human Research Program pages. It answers spoken questions in plain language, always names its source, and refuses when the sources do not cover the question. Alert levels come from coded rules, never from the AI, and the tool states that it is not a diagnosis.

Astronauts must often detect health changes themselves, far from doctors. Voice frees their hands, and sourced answers make advice traceable. The assistant’s logic runs without internet. Thresholds and data are simulated hypotheses, not medical advice.
details:
What it does and how it works. Our project is a concept for smart health glasses that help astronauts on long missions monitor their immune health hands-free. Sensors in the frame would measure skin temperature, resting pulse and cabin CO2, while sleep, symptoms and blood test values would be logged by voice. We had no hardware and no hardware simulator, so the sensor values are generated by simulation code written directly in the web interface and in a Python backend. The voice assistant is the part we built and tested separately. It takes a spoken sentence (transcribed to text) and either answers a question, reads the astronaut’s current state, explains an alert, logs a symptom, a sleep duration or a measured value, or undoes the last entry. Answers come from six explanation cards written from 15 NASA and Canadian Space Agency pages, found with multilingual embeddings. Every answer names its source. If the sources do not cover the question, for example the normal blood pressure, the assistant refuses. Alert levels are computed by coded rules, never by the AI.

Benefits. Astronauts far from Earth must often detect health changes themselves, with delayed contact with doctors. Voice use works with gloves and in microgravity, sourced answers make advice traceable, and the assistant’s logic runs without internet. It cannot invent facts, give a diagnosis or suggest a drug.

Expected impact. With real sensors and medical review, such a tool could help crews notice immune-related changes earlier and understand what NASA research says about them. The same approach could support isolated places on Earth where doctors are far away. We make no clinical claim: our data and thresholds are simulated hypotheses, not medical advice.

Tools. Python for the backend, the data collection and the voice assistant; a web frontend for the interface; Google Colab (CPU) with requests and BeautifulSoup to collect the NASA pages; sentence-transformers with the BAAI/bge-m3 model for retrieval; JSON files for the explanation cards; and a test suite of 19 cases for the assistant. No physical hardware or hardware simulator was used: sensor data are simulated directly in code. We also prepared a local language model stage (Qwen2.5-7B) but did not use it for final answers, because no GPU was available and a source-only, rule-based design is safer.

Creativity. The idea of sensing glasses is not new: research prototypes exist and NASA has used HoloLens headsets on the ISS. What is new in our approach is the combination of an immune focus, voice-first use, answers that must cite NASA sources and can refuse, and a strict split where rules decide and the assistant only explains. The design follows NASA’s statement that spaceflight hazards are not independent and can worsen one another, so it considers temperature, resting pulse, sleep and CO2 together.

Factors considered. Safety (no diagnosis, no medication advice, human review of every explanation card), honesty about what is simulated and what is hypothesis, traceability of sources, hands-free use, offline operation of the assistant, and privacy (no real health data). We also recognize known limits: skin temperature is not core body temperature, two cards rely on team summaries that must be checked against the original studies, and the voice recognition of a browser usually needs an internet connection. We worked under tight constraints: less than 24 hours, no hardware, no GPU, and a team that split the work between the interface, the backend, the immune module and the retrieval assistant.
